title: Bapuji Cake: West Bengal's ₹8 Tiffin Icon Still Sells 50,000 a Day
excerpt: New Howrah Bakery's humble square of buttered sponge has fed West Bengal's tea breaks since 1973 — handmade, sold for a handful of rupees, and still moving tens of thousands of pieces a day.
body:
• Bapuji Cake, made by New Howrah Bakery since 1973, remains a beloved West Bengal tea-time staple sold at roadside tea stalls across the state.
  • The bakery, run by brothers Amitava and Animesh Jana, produces around 50,000 tiffin cakes a day — mostly by hand — in workshops in Howrah, Serampore and Lake Town.
  • The no-frills square buttered cake, studded with tutti frutti and petha, sells for a handful of rupees in minimalist paper packaging.
  • NDTV Food's spotlight this week put the cake's staying power back in the public eye, against far fancier competition.

A tea-stall classic gets its moment

Some snacks never leave the glass jar. This week, NDTV Food's feature on Bapuji Cake — the unassuming square of buttered sponge that has accompanied West Bengal's tea breaks for more than five decades — has put one of Kolkata's most enduring edible icons back in the spotlight. No frosting, no filling, no celebrity endorsement. Just a simple tiffin cake that has outlasted every bakery trend that tried to displace it.

The cake is the flagship product of New Howrah Bakery Pvt. Ltd., a family-run company founded in 1973 by the father of brothers Amitava and Animesh Jana, who run it today. The bakery's office sits in the unassuming Howrah neighbourhood of Pallabpukur, with production spread across workshops in Howrah, Serampore in Hooghly district, and Kolkata's Lake Town area, according to a Hindu BusinessLine profile.

The scale belies the modest setup. "Ours is a small-scale operation and our cakes are made manually to a large extent," Amitava Jana told BusinessLine, adding that the bakery sells an average of 50,000 tiffin cakes a day in and around Kolkata, "and our popularity is on the rise".

"For the common man, tiffin cakes have now become synonymous with Bapuji, just like all chocolate bars have come to be referred to as Cadbury's."

— Amitava Jana, co-owner, New Howrah Bakery

Context & Background

Bapuji Cake's staying power is rooted in its no-frills character. Traditionally a square, buttered slice enriched with tutti frutti and pieces of petha — ash gourd candy — it arrives in minimalist paper packaging and sells for a handful of rupees; Bengali grocery sellers list it at around ₹10 a piece. At any roadside tea stall in Kolkata, glass jars of the cake are "always flying off the shelves," as Indulge Express put it.

Its ubiquity made it the default. Bapuji became a favourite accompaniment to afternoon tea at roadside shacks — second in popularity only to the invincible deem-paunruti, or bread-and-eggs — a compulsory part of picnic breakfast packs and the dependable snack that even the fussiest middle-class Bengali mother would pack into a school lunch box, BusinessLine reported.

Impact & Analysis

The cake's survival is remarkable given the churn around it. The 1980s and 90s belonged to brands like Farinni, whose Double Bite range was a household favourite before vanishing from shelves; today, French patisseries dominate Kolkata with opera cakes and mousses, and dry cakes have become a scarce sight, according to Indulge Express. Bapuji, meanwhile, never tried to compete on glamour — and never had to.

Part of the appeal is what the brand never did: it has reportedly never been advertised, yet its popularity holds steady, sustained by tea shops, tiffin boxes, bus stops and railway stations. The minimalist paper packaging also doubles as an eco-friendly touch that loyal customers still praise.

The road has not been entirely smooth. Recent customer reviews on travel and food listings flag inconsistent quality and poor packaging in some batches — a reminder that a 50-year-old handmade operation turning out tens of thousands of cakes a day faces the same quality-control pressures as any food business. Yet the loyal base persists: as Indulge Express noted, the cake reflects "the practicality and warmth of Kolkata's working-class ethos," and that identity has proved harder to dislodge than any competitor.

Diaspora Angle

For Bengalis who grew up in West Bengal and now live elsewhere, Bapuji Cake is pure nostalgia fuel — the taste of a school tiffin box, a platform tea stall, a grandmother's kitchen shelf. Indian e-commerce sellers now list multi-packs for buyers chasing that memory outside Kolkata, making the cake one of those foods that travels in suitcases on every homecoming.

What's Next

Bapuji Cake shows no signs of slowing. Amitava Jana's own assessment — that sales are on the rise — suggests the brand's 53-year run still has room to grow, and the NDTV Food spotlight may introduce the cake to a generation that missed the tiffin-box years. Whether the bakery can maintain handmade consistency at such volumes will decide whether the next 50 years look like the last 50 — a question its most loyal customers are already watching closely.
